stem: A validator backtests a PD model that predicted a 5% one-year default rate for 1,000 independent obligors. Observed defaults were 68. Using the normal approximation to the binomial, the z-statistic for the calibration test is closest to:
explanation: Expected defaults = 1,000 × 0.05 = 50. Standard deviation = √(1,000 × 0.05 × 0.95) = √47.5 = 6.892. z = (68 − 50) / 6.892 = 2.61, which exceeds 1.96, so calibration is rejected at the 5% level.

rationale.A: Incorrect. 2.26 uses the observed default rate of 6.8% in the variance instead of the predicted 5% under the null hypothesis.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 0.38 divides by the variance 47.5 instead of its square root.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 2.55 uses √(nP) as the standard deviation (a Poisson approximation), omitting the (1 − P) term.

stem: A bank applies a well-validated residential mortgage PD model to price loans to commercial real estate developers. The resulting model risk is best described as arising from:
options: a coding error in the model implementation
inadequate data quality in the development sample
misuse of the model outside its intended scope
an incorrect theoretical foundation for mortgage default
explanation: The model may be sound for residential mortgages; the risk comes from using it on a population it was not built for, which is misuse.

rationale.A: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the code is wrong.
rationale.B: Incorrect. The data may be fine for the intended population; the problem is the application.
rationale.C: Correct. Applying a model outside its intended scope is misuse.
rationale.D: Incorrect. The theory may be appropriate for residential mortgages.

stem: Which arrangement best satisfies the principle of effective challenge in model validation?
options: The developers who built the model perform the validation because they understand it best
A separate team with relevant quantitative skills and authority to restrict model use performs the validation
The model's business users sign off on the model after confirming its outputs look reasonable
The vendor's own validation report is accepted without further review
explanation: Effective challenge requires competence, independence and influence. A separate, skilled team with authority to restrict use meets all three; developers, users and vendors lack independence.

rationale.A: Incorrect. Developers are not independent of their own work.
rationale.B: Correct. Competence, independence and authority together constitute effective challenge.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Users have an interest in the model and a reasonableness check is not a validation.
rationale.D: Incorrect. Vendor models still require the bank's own validation, such as benchmarking and outcomes analysis.

stem: A bank has 600 models and a small validation team. Which approach is most consistent with sound model risk management?
options: Validate all 600 models with identical depth every year
Validate only models used for regulatory capital and exclude all others from the inventory
Rely on internal audit to perform model validations in place of a validation function
Maintain a complete inventory, tier models by materiality and complexity, and set validation depth and frequency by tier
explanation: A complete inventory with risk-based tiering lets a bank focus scarce validation resources on the most material and complex models while still covering every model at an appropriate depth.

rationale.A: Incorrect. Uniform depth wastes resources on immaterial models and starves high-risk ones.
rationale.B: Incorrect. Non-regulatory models such as pricing or provisioning tools can also cause large losses and must be inventoried.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Internal audit reviews the framework; it does not replace independent validation.
rationale.D: Correct. Inventory plus risk-based tiering is the standard approach.
